text: Alfred Robert Bader CBE (April 28, 1924 – December 23, 2018) was a Canadian chemist, businessman, philanthropist, and collector of fine art. He was recognized by the Chemical & Engineering News poll of 1998 as one of the "Top 75 Distinguished Contributors to the Chemical Enterprise" during the journal's 75-year history. Born in Vienna, Austria, on April 28, 1924, Bader’s father was of Czech Jewish descent, and his grandfather, Moriz Bader, was a civil engineer who worked on the Suez Canal and was appointed Knight of the Order of Franz Joseph by Emperor Franz Joseph for his service as Austrian consul at Ismaïlia. His mother, Elizabeth Countess Serényi, came from an aristocratic Catholic Hungarian family. Despite opposition from her family, the couple married in London and settled in Vienna. Alfred was born two weeks before his father's death and was adopted by his father's sister, Gisela Reich, and raised as a Jew. His older sister, Marion, remained with Countess Serényi and was raised as a Catholic. In June 1938, Bader was expelled from school because Jews were barred from attending beyond age 14. On December 10, 1938, he was sent to England via the Kindertransport to escape Nazi persecution; his adoptive mother remained in Austria and died in 1942 in Theresienstadt. While in England, he attended East Hove Senior School for Boys and Brighton Technical College. In 1940, he was sent to a Canadian internment camp for European refugees, which he described as spartan but beneficial to his academic and social development. There, he passed his junior and senior matriculation exams from McGill University. A Montreal sponsor, Martin Wolff, welcomed him into a Canadian Jewish family in late 1941 and encouraged his further studies. After being rejected by McGill due to its Jewish quota and by the University of Toronto, where the chemistry department was engaged in sensitive war work, Bader was accepted by Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario. He earned a B.Sc. in Engineering Chemistry in 1945 and a B.A. in history in 1946. During summers, he worked for the Murphy Paint Company in Montreal, formulating paints, lacquers, and varnishes. He completed his M.S. in chemistry in 1947, conducting significant research on the oxidation of linoleic acids and isomeric tetrahydroxystearic acids under the supervision of Arthur F. McKay, a "superb experimentalist," which led him to focus on synthetic organic chemistry. With support from the Abbott fellowship, Bader studied at Harvard University, receiving an M.A. in chemistry in 1949 and a Ph.D. in Organic Chemistry in 1950. At Harvard, he worked with renowned organic chemist Louis Fieser on the rearrangement of quinones and the development of intermediates in the Hooker oxidation process. While at Murphy Paint, Bader was offered financial support for graduate study on the condition he return to work at the company. When he completed his Ph.D., Murphy Paint had been acquired by Pittsburgh Plate Glass Co. In January 1950, Bader began as a research chemist at PPG in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, breaking an unwritten rule against hiring Jews and African Americans. At PPG, he conducted significant work in noncatalytic transesterification and monomer development, including systematic studies of alkenylphenols, unsaturated phenols, and phenolic resins, leading to numerous patents. The patent for Bader’s method of creating diphenolic acid was later sold by PPG to Johnson Wax for $1 million. He remained with PPG until 1954, when the company planned a move to Pittsburgh. During this time, Bader recognized the need for a reliable supplier of research chemicals, noting that Kodak was the only supplier at the time and often failed to meet researchers’ needs, a problem he experienced personally as a graduate student. In 1951, while still employed at PPG, Bader co-founded the Aldrich Chemical Company with Jack Eisendrath, a lawyer, who became the first company president. Although Bader held the title of Chief Chemist, most chemicals were not produced in-house; instead, he sourced compounds from various U.S. and European suppliers and listed them in a catalog. The company initially operated from a garage where chemicals were stored and packaged for mailing. The first product shipped was Methylnitronitrosoguanidine, which Bader had learned to produce at Queen's. By 1954, Bader and his first wife, Helen "Danny" Daniels, bought Eisendrath out of Aldrich, becoming "sole and equal owners" of the company. Bader became the company president and left PPG. The Aldrich Chemical Company catalog eventually grew to contain nearly 50,000 substances, described by the Chemical Heritage Foundation as "a huge library of rare chemicals," and its "Big Red" annual catalog was widely used as a reference due to its extensive physical and structural data. As the catalog expanded, so did the company. In 1962, in a 50:50 venture with Metal Hydrides Inc., Bader founded Alfa Inorganics to complement Aldrich’s organic chemicals, though the joint venture was terminated in 1967. A separate corporation, the Alfred Bader Chemical Corp., was sold to Aldrich on December 20, 1965. A British subsidiary, originally known as Ralph N. Emanuel, Ltd., was co-owned by the Emanuel and Bader families from 1959 to 1969 and was gradually taken over by Aldrich, officially renamed Aldrich Chemical Co. Ltd. in 1973. Aldrich obtained a controlling interest in Heidenheimer Chemisches Laboratorium (HCL) in Heidenheim, Germany by 1971. In 1975, Aldrich merged with Sigma Chemical Corporation to form the Sigma-Aldrich Corporation, combining Aldrich’s leadership in organic research chemicals with Sigma’s strength in research biochemicals, becoming the 80th largest chemical company in the United States. As of 1987, 35% of Aldrich’s chemicals were produced in-house. Bader served as president from 1975 to 1980 and as chairman from 1980 to 1991, retiring as chairman in 1991 and being named chairman emeritus. In 1992, he was voted off the board, losing the title of chairman emeritus, though he remained one of the largest stockholders. Bader later stated that while the change was a significant blow, it gave him more time to focus on art collecting and philanthropy, making him happier. The company later reinstated him as "chemist collector," providing paintings for the covers of the company journal, Aldrichimica Acta. Bader described himself as an "inveterate collector," beginning with stamps at age eight, drawings at ten, paintings at twenty, and rare chemicals at thirty. As a youth, he collected stamps when financially able. In the Canadian internment camp, he purchased his first oil painting—a portrait of himself by a fellow inmate—for one Canadian dollar. A lifelong collector, Bader established Alfred Bader Fine Arts gallery in Milwaukee in 1961 with Marvin Klitsner. Beginning with its first issue in 1968, he contributed numerous articles on art to Aldrichimica Acta, and full-color copies of Dutch masters from his collection were used for journal covers. Artworks from his collection were also featured in the Aldrich Handbook, starting with the Quill Cutter by Paulus de Lesire in the 1967–68 edition. In 1995, Bader published his autobiography, Adventures of a Chemist Collector, detailing his journey from a Nazi-era refugee to a chemist magnate and fine arts connoisseur. In 2008, he published a second autobiography, Chemistry & Art – Further Adventures of a Chemist Collector. Bader died at home in Milwaukee on December 23, 2018. He made various charitable donations to Queen's University, Canada, including purchasing the 15th-century Herstmonceux Castle in East Sussex, England, which he donated to Queen's University and opened as Bader College in 1994. The residence at the castle is named "Bader Hall." Bader and his second wife, Isabel, established several fellowships, including the Alfred Bader Graduate Fellowship, the Alfred Bader Graduate Fellowship in Art, the Alfred Bader Graduate Fellowship in the Humanities, and the Alfred and Isabel Bader Postdoctoral Fellowship in Jewish History. Queen's also hosts three Bader Chairs: in Organic Chemistry, in Southern Baroque Art, and in Northern Baroque Art. In 2004, Queen's renamed a campus road from "Queen's Crescent" to "Bader Lane" in recognition of his contributions. The Baders are long-time supporters of the Agnes Etherington Art Centre at Queen's in Kingston, Ontario. Upon invitation from curator Frances Smith in 1967, Bader first donated a painting to Queen's, a Salvator Mundi. In 2014, he and Isabel donated 68 paintings from their personal collection of Dutch and Flemish Baroque art to the Agnes Etherington Art Centre, bringing the total number of paintings donated to over 200. Highlights include three Rembrandt van Rijn paintings: Head of an Old Man in a Cap, Head of a Man in a Turban, and Portrait of a Man with Arms Akimbo, as well as works by Willem Drost, Jan Lievens, Aert de Gelder, and Jacobus Leveck. The collection has been the basis for numerous exhibitions and publications. The Baders also made a "transformational gift" toward the creation of the Isabel Bader Centre for the Performing Arts, which opened in 2014. The center includes a music performance hall, studio theatre, small cinema, art and media lab, large rehearsal hall, and classrooms, bringing together the Department of Film and Media, the School of Music, the Department of Drama, and the Bachelor of Fine Art Program at Queen's, providing performance venues for both the university and the surrounding city. At Victoria University in Toronto, the alma mater of Isabel Bader, the Baders funded the construction of the Isabel Bader Theatre. They also supported Project SEED, an American Chemical Society initiative providing scholarships to economically disadvantaged high school students and enabling hands-on research. Since 2001, they have supported the Malta Conferences Foundation, using science as a bridge to peace in the Middle East. Since 1986, they have funded the Alfred Bader Award in Bioinorganic or Bioorganic Chemistry by the American Chemical Society to recognize outstanding contributions in those fields. Since 1989, they have funded the Bader Award from the Royal Society of Chemistry to recognize eminence in organic chemistry. Since 2013, the Alfred Bader Award has been given by the Canadian Society for Chemistry to a Canadian scientist for excellence in organic chemistry research. As of 2011, the Baders donated $1.6 million toward the construction of the Kenwood Interdisciplinary Research Complex (KIRC) at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee. Awards and honors received by Bader include, but are not limited to, the following. His marriages are detailed in his autobiographies. His romance with Isabel Overton (1926–2022), daughter of a deeply religious Protestant family in Northern Ontario and a Victoria University graduate in Toronto, began with a shipboard meeting in 1949 and continued through a rapid courtship involving some 400 love letters. Isabel broke off the relationship due to religious concerns and settled in Bexhill-on-Sea, England, without becoming romantically involved with anyone else. Her love letters to Bader were published as A Canadian in Love in 2000. Bader married his first wife, Helen Ann "Danny" Daniels, in the United States. Similar to Isabel, Daniels had a Protestant upbringing and converted to Judaism before Bader proposed. They married in July 1952 and had two sons, David (born 1958) and Daniel (born 1961). Daniels worked at Aldrich Chemicals and owned shares in the company. Nearly three decades later, Bader reconnected with Isabel, leading to the breakdown of his marriage with Daniels, who requested a divorce in 1981 and died six years later. Bader subsequently married Isabel, and the two remained happily married until his death. Bader and Daniels’ sons, David and Daniel, now serve as half-owners of Alfred Bader Fine Arts. (Descendants of Bader’s former partner in that gallery, Marvin Klitsner, now own the other half.) They also serve as president and vice-president of Bader Philanthropies, a foundation formed in 1992 to honor Helen Daniels Bader and Isabel and Alfred Bader.
